### Seed to seed, what the seed savers know

Suzanne Ashworth, a Sacramento grower, wrote Seed to Seed in 1991 for Seed Savers Exchange, founded in 1975 by Diane Ott Whealy and Kent Whealy to keep family seed alive. Three of its ideas shape how we save seed with children.

- **Open pollinated seed comes true.** A plant grown from heirloom seed makes seed that grows the same plant. A hybrid, bred by crossing two parents, does not. That is why our seed library is heirloom and why a packet a child labels this fall can be planted next spring with trust.
- **Some plants cross.** Squash, corn and brassicas cross readily with neighbors of their kind, while beans, peas, lettuce and tomatoes mostly pollinate themselves. We save first from the plants that keep to themselves, so children see the circle close.
- **Dry seed and wet seed.** Beans, lettuce, poppies and calendula dry on the plant. Tomato and cucumber seed sits in wet pulp and is rinsed, and tomato seed is left to ferment a few days first. Both kinds dry fully before they go into paper.

Robin Wall Kimmerer's Honorable Harvest sits beside Ashworth's method. Saved seed is the gift we give back, and Leah Penniman reminds us that seed carries the stories of everyone who saved it before. The Idea bank card Seed to seed follows one plant all the way round and closes with a family seed swap.

### How children come to understand a cycle

Jean Piaget found in the 1940s that young children judge time by what they can see, so a plant that grew taller took longer, whatever the calendar said. William Friedman at Oberlin College showed across the 1980s and 1990s that children learn the order of a day first, the week later, and the year as a circle in the early school years. Anne Hickling and Susan Gelman found in 1995 that most four year olds know a seed grows into a plant of its own kind, and the full return to seed is held best by children who have watched it.

- **Twos and threes.** The harvest is now. A berry found under a leaf, a bean pod opened, seeds poured from hand to hand. The cycle is lived in the body, and holding it in mind comes later.
- **Threes and fours.** Before and after. A flower that was there last week is a pod this week, and children can say what happened. A ribbon on one flower followed to a berry gives one thread to watch.
- **Fours, fives and TK.** Seed to seed as a story with a beginning, a middle and a return. Children draw the stages in order, predict what comes next, and plant seed they saved themselves. The orchard book and the strawberry year book hold a whole year on the wall.

Being there for the whole of it is what teaches a cycle, so we leave plants in the bed to go to seed where children can visit them. The Idea bank cards The orchard through the year and Strawberries hold the monthly return to one spot.

### Keeping food, a short history

People have kept food since before farming. Drying in sun and wind is the oldest way and the one we use most. Pomo and Coast Miwok people stored acorns in raised granaries through the winter and dried fish, seeds and berries. Salt, smoke and fermentation came with settled life, and sauerkraut, pickles and cheese are foods kept by friendly microbes. Nicolas Appert in France showed in 1810 that food sealed in a jar and heated would keep, decades before Louis Pasteur explained why, and John Landis Mason patented the screw top jar in 1858. Home freezing came in the twentieth century.

Drying and tea are ours. Canning for storage asks for exact times and pressures to keep botulism out, and the UC Master Food Preserver program carries the current rules, so we do not can for storage with children. The Idea bank card Herbs and tea holds the bundling, drying and daily checks.

### Saving seed

### How children learn to like a food

Leann Birch, a developmental psychologist, spent thirty years at the University of Illinois and Penn State studying how children come to eat what they eat. In 1982 she and Diane Marlin offered two year olds unfamiliar fruits and cheeses on different numbers of days and found that liking rose with the number of tastes. Later studies with preschoolers and vegetables put the number at eight to fifteen tastes (repeated exposure), with a taste counting more than a look or a smell. A child who refuses kale the first six times is on schedule.

Birch also found what gets in the way. In 1984 she showed that children offered a reward for eating a food liked that food less afterward, and in 1999 Jennifer Fisher and Birch found that keeping a food out of reach made children want it more and eat more of it when they could. Pressure to eat and rewards for eating both work against the child. The wariness itself, a pulling back from new foods (food neophobia), is strongest between about two and six and eases with age, and that is the whole span of our program.

Ellyn Satter, a dietitian and family therapist, turned this into a plain rule in the 1980s (the division of responsibility in feeding). Adults decide what food is offered, when and where. The child decides whether to eat it and how much. At our table that means the garden food children made sits beside what the Kitchen planned, every child is offered it, and no one is asked to try a bite.

### What cooking asks of a child

Cooking with children is often claimed for math and literacy, and the fit is plain. A recipe is read in order, ingredients are counted and measured, halves and wholes are seen in a cut apple, and a batter changes in front of the child. The research is thinner than the claim. A 2014 review by Derek Hersch and colleagues for the Centers for Disease Control found that cooking programs for school age children raised their willingness to taste and their confidence in the kitchen, and that most studies were short and could not show lasting change. Leslie Cunningham-Sabo's Cooking with Kids program in New Mexico reported in 2013 that fourth graders who cooked preferred more vegetables and felt more able to cook than those who only tasted. We say that cooking gives children a reason to count, read and measure, and we document what they do with it rather than claim more.

Alice Waters, who began the Edible Schoolyard in 1995, writes that the senses are the way into the mind, and that a child who has smelled basil in the bed and torn it over a bowl knows something no lesson can give. Our Early Plate idea says the same thing in our own words. Food is handled with respect from bed to bowl, it is prepared simply, and it is never an art or sensory material, because a child who paints with pudding learns that food is for playing with. The Idea bank cards Cooking and food and Piazza and culinary atelier hold the grips, the tools and the agreements.

### How cooking grows by age

- **Twos and threes.** Washing, tearing, squeezing and stirring. One tool at a time. Tasting is offered and never required, since this is when wariness is highest. Food as a job in the hands, carrying the bowl to the table.
- **Threes and fours.** The bridge grip and the claw grip on soft foods with a serrated tomato knife, one child per knife, seated at the board. Taste tests with children's words written down. A recipe followed as pictures.
- **Fours, fives and TK.** A mini santoku and harder foods with an adult beside them. Recipes read and scaled, the Unicorn Café with menus and prices, a class cookbook, and one plant grown, cooked and saved for seed across the year.

### Attachment, and the people who shaped care for the youngest

John Bowlby, a British psychiatrist, proposed from the 1950s on that a young child is built to stay close to a few particular adults and to use them as a safe place to leave from and return to (attachment, and the secure base). Mary Ainsworth reported in 1978 on Baltimore mothers and one year olds watched at home and then in a short separation and reunion (the Strange Situation). The children who explored most freely were those whose adults had answered their signals promptly and warmly through the first year (sensitive responsiveness). Later research found that a child can form a secure attachment to a steady, responsive educator too, and that bond adds to the one at home. This is the ground under primary caregiving in West class.

Emmi Pikler, a Hungarian pediatrician, ran a residential nursery in Budapest from 1946. Her records showed that infants left to move freely, never propped or placed in positions they could not get into themselves, reached the motor milestones in their own order and time. She paired that freedom with full, unhurried attention during care. Magda Gerber brought Pikler's ideas to California and in 1978 founded Resources for Infant Educarers (RIE). Her practice asks adults to tell a child what will happen before it happens, to wait, and to watch without stepping in.

J. Ronald Lally built WestEd's PITC program from 1985 on these foundations and named six program practices that quality rests on. Primary care, small groups, continuity of care across years, care that follows each child's rhythm (individualized care), care that honors each family's culture (cultural continuity) and inclusion of children with disabilities. Our three year arc with the same educators is continuity of care.

Alison Gopnik at the University of California, Berkeley has shown that very young children test ideas by trying things and watching what happens (hypothesis testing), and that their attention is wide and open where an adult's narrows to one thing. In The Gardener and the Carpenter, 2016, she asks adults to tend the conditions a child grows in and warns against shaping a child to a plan.

### Two year olds by domain

Erik Erikson placed ages one to three in the work of doing things for oneself and feeling capable doing them (autonomy versus shame and doubt), so "me do it" and the refusals of this age are development doing its work. Every child's path through the year is their own.

- **Body.** Running, climbing, kicking a ball, stairs with a hand and then alone. Jumping with both feet comes toward three. Falls are frequent while balance grows.
- **Hands.** A tower of six blocks near two and eight or more by three, pages turned one at a time, a spoon and a cup managed, scribbles that become circles and lines by three, the finger and thumb grip (pincer grasp) refined on every small thing.
- **Language.** About fifty words at two, two word phrases soon after, and by three short sentences and a vocabulary in the hundreds. Children understand far more than they say, and gesture, face and sound carry much of what they mean.
- **Thinking.** The first pretend, a block held as a phone (symbolic play), sorting by one feature, matching, and a strong memory for where things live. Routines are predicted and protested when changed.
- **Self and feelings.** Self recognition in a mirror by about two, then "I" and "mine". Big feelings spill into the body as crying, hitting, running, going still or clinging (dysregulation), and each one is a signal to read. The child needs a steady adult to borrow from (co-regulation).
- **With others.** Playing beside another child (parallel play), watching closely, offering a toy and taking it back, noticing when someone is sad. Friendship begins here.

West class holds children from two to nearly four, so both ends of this list sit at the same table and the environment serves both. The Idea bank cards Something to carry, The same song for moving, Sorting a big basket and The covered table with one material hold set-ups made for this year.

### Care is curriculum
